# Feature Development Workflow

All non-trivial features follow this 11-phase gate process. Do not advance to the next phase without explicit sign-off from the user.

**Before creating, modifying, or deleting any file** — docs, code, or config — check that a feature branch (`feature/<short-name>`) is already checked out. If it is not, create and check it out first.

| # | Phase | Summary |
|---|-------|---------|
| 0 | [Pre-flight](#phase-0--pre-flight) | Clean install, update workflow docs if outdated |
| 1 | [Brainstorm](#phase-1--brainstorm) | Explore ideas and surface trade-offs; no code or design yet |
| 2 | [Requirements](#phase-2--requirements) | Define in-scope / out-of-scope; get explicit sign-off |
| 3 | [Design](#phase-3--design) | Document files, interfaces, data flow; prose only |
| 4 | [Tasks](#phase-4--tasks) | Break design into ordered, self-contained tasks |
| 5 | [Implement](#phase-5--implement) | Execute tasks via Haiku subagent |
| 6 | [Review](#phase-6--review) | Check requirements, security, and documentation against the diff |
| 7 | [Log Changes](#phase-7--log-changes) | Produce change log from the completed diff |
| 8 | [Commit](#phase-8--commit) | Run checks, stage files, confirm commit message |
| 9 | [PR](#phase-9--pr) | Draft and open the pull request |
| 10 | [Close](#phase-10--close) | Confirm merge, switch to main, delete local feature branch |

---

## Feature Documentation

Each feature gets its own folder under `docs/specs/features/<feature-name>/`. Create the folder at the start of Phase 1 and add a file per phase as work progresses. Only phases that produce meaningful output need a file.

```
docs/specs/features/<feature-name>/
  01-brainstorm.md    # Ideas explored, direction chosen
  02-requirements.md  # In-scope / out-of-scope list, agreed by user
  03-design.md        # Files, interfaces, data flow, decisions
  04-tasks.md         # Ordered task list
  06-review.md        # Review findings and resolutions
  07-changes.md       # Change log after implementation
  progress.md         # Running log of every change made during the feature
```

**Naming:** use `kebab-case` for `<feature-name>`, matching the feature branch name — e.g. folder `docs/specs/features/price-alerts/` maps to branch `feature/price-alerts`.

**When to write each file:** at the end of the phase, once the user has signed off. Keep them concise — they are a record of decisions, not a narrative retelling of the conversation.

**`progress.md`** is written continuously during implementation (Phase 5 onward). Only log things worth knowing after the fact — not every file touched. Record:

- **Decisions** — non-obvious choices made during implementation and why
- **Blockers** — problems encountered, what was tried, and how they were resolved
- **Test failures** — what failed, root cause, and the fix applied
- **Deviations** — anything that diverged from the agreed design and why

Format:

```markdown
## YYYY-MM-DD

- Decision: [what was decided and why]
- Blocker: [problem] → [resolution]
- Test failure: [what failed] → [root cause] → [fix]
- Deviation: [what differed from the design and why]
```

## Phase 0 — Pre-flight

Before starting any feature work, ensure the project is in a clean, up-to-date state.

1. **Clean install** — run `npm ci` to reset dependencies to the lockfile. In a monorepo (workspace root), always run this from the root, not from inside a package directory.
2. **Check for a newer `@robproper/feature-workflow`** — run `npm outdated @robproper/feature-workflow`. If a newer version is available, install it immediately: `npm install @robproper/feature-workflow@latest`. This overwrites the workflow docs in `docs/` with the latest versions and patches `CLAUDE.md` as needed.
3. **Confirm you are on `main` and it is up to date** — run `git checkout main && git pull` before creating the feature branch.

> "Running pre-flight: clean install, checking for workflow updates, confirming main is current."

No user sign-off needed — proceed to Phase 1 once these steps complete cleanly.

[↑ Back to top](#feature-development-workflow)

## Phase 1 — Brainstorm

Explore ideas and surface trade-offs. Do not propose a design or write any code. Ask open questions. End with a short summary of the leading direction and invite the user to narrow it down.

> "Let's brainstorm [feature]. Here are a few angles: [2–4 options with trade-offs]. What resonates, or is there a direction I'm missing?"

[↑ Back to top](#feature-development-workflow)

---

## Phase 2 — Requirements

Translate the agreed direction into a concrete, unambiguous requirements list. Distinguish in-scope items from out-of-scope. Get explicit user sign-off before proceeding.

> "Based on the brainstorm, here are the requirements:
> **In scope:** [list]
> **Out of scope:** [list]
> Does this match your intent, or should we adjust anything?"

[↑ Back to top](#feature-development-workflow)

---

## Phase 3 — Design

Document the proposed design: new/changed files, key interfaces, data flow, and any non-obvious decisions. No code yet — prose and pseudocode only. Get sign-off.

> "Here's the proposed design:
> **New files:** [list]
> **Changed files:** [list with reason]
> **Key interfaces / data flow:** [description]
> **Trade-offs / decisions:** [notes]
> Ready to proceed, or should we adjust the design?"

[↑ Back to top](#feature-development-workflow)

---

## Phase 4 — Tasks

Break the design into ordered, discrete tasks. Each task should be completable independently. Present the list and get confirmation before starting.

**Task detail standard — write for Haiku.** Each task must be self-contained and explicit enough that `claude-haiku-5-5` can execute it without needing context from earlier phases. This means every task must include:
- The exact files to create or modify (relative paths)
- The interfaces or types it consumes and produces
- Key constraints, edge cases, and error conditions to handle
- The test cases to write (input → expected output)
- The exact shell command to verify it (type-check or lint run)

If a task requires judgment or design decisions, resolve them here — do not leave them for the implementer.

> "Here are the implementation tasks in order: [list]. Any additions or re-ordering before I start?"

[↑ Back to top](#feature-development-workflow)

---

## Phase 5 — Implement

**Model: `claude-haiku-5-5`** — delegate implementation to Haiku via a subagent. Tasks must already be detailed enough (Phase 4) that Haiku can execute them without clarification.

Work task by task, marking each done as you go. No scope creep — if new work surfaces, add it as a new task and flag it to the user.

> "Creating branch `feature/<name>` and starting implementation. I'll update you at each milestone."

[↑ Back to top](#feature-development-workflow)

## Phase 6 — Review

**Model: `claude-sonnet-5-5`** — use Sonnet, not Haiku. Review requires careful reasoning about edge cases, security implications, and subtle requirement gaps. Haiku is optimised for fast execution and misses nuanced issues; Opus is thorough but expensive for a task that runs once per feature. Sonnet provides the right balance of analytical depth and cost.

Review the diff against three lenses — requirements, security, and documentation. The review focuses on **what changed**; existing code is used only as context, not as a target.

### What to read — and what not to

**Read:**
- `git diff main...HEAD` — the diff is the primary input; everything else is context
- `docs/specs/features/<feature-name>/02-requirements.md` — the agreed in-scope / out-of-scope list
- `docs/specs/requirements.md` — overall system requirements, if the file exists
- `docs/specs/design.md` — overall system design, if the file exists

**Do not read** (these describe how the feature was planned and built, not what it must do):
- `docs/specs/features/<feature-name>/01-brainstorm.md`
- `docs/specs/features/<feature-name>/03-design.md`
- `docs/specs/features/<feature-name>/04-tasks.md`
- `docs/specs/features/<feature-name>/progress.md`
- `docs/specs/features/<feature-name>/06-changes.md` (not yet written at this point)

Reading the feature's own design and task documents biases the review toward what was planned rather than what was actually built and whether it satisfies the requirements. The overall system docs (`docs/specs/requirements.md`, `docs/specs/design.md`) provide legitimate broader context without that bias.

### How to review

1. **Get the diff** — run `git diff main...HEAD` to see all changes on the feature branch.
2. **Requirements check** — read `docs/specs/features/<feature-name>/02-requirements.md` and, if present, `docs/specs/requirements.md`. For each in-scope item, verify the changed code satisfies it. Flag any requirement that is missing or only partially met.
3. **Security check** — scan the changed lines for common issues: injection vulnerabilities (SQL, command, path traversal), unsafe use of user-supplied input, secrets or credentials in code, broken access control, insecure defaults, missing input validation at system boundaries.
4. **Documentation check** — verify that changed public interfaces, non-obvious logic, and new configuration options are adequately documented (types, inline comments for the *why*, updated `docs/` files if behaviour changed).

### Findings format

Categorise each finding as one of:

| Category | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `blocker` | Must be fixed before proceeding — incorrect behaviour, security risk, or unmet requirement |
| `advisory` | Recommended improvement — does not block the phase but should be addressed soon |

For each finding, record:
- **Category** — `blocker` or `advisory`
- **File and line** — exact location in the diff
- **Description** — what is wrong and why it matters
- **Suggestion** — concrete fix

### Outcomes

- **No blockers** — present any advisories to the user, then proceed to Phase 7 with sign-off.
- **One or more blockers** — return to **Phase 5 — Implement** to fix each blocker. Re-run the review after fixes are committed.

Save findings to `docs/specs/features/<feature-name>/06-review.md`. If there are no findings, write a one-line entry confirming the review was completed clean.

> "Review complete. Blockers: [n]. Advisories: [n].
> [Finding list or 'No issues found.']
> [If blockers: 'Returning to Phase 5 to fix blockers before proceeding.']
> [If clean: 'Ready to proceed to Phase 7 — Log Changes.']"

## Phase 7 — Log Changes

**Model: `claude-haiku-5-5`** — Haiku generates the change log from the completed diff.

After implementation and review are complete, produce a concise change log: new files, modified files, key decisions made during implementation, and anything that deviated from the design.

> "Implementation complete. Here's what changed:
> **New:** [files]
> **Modified:** [files + one-line reason]
> **Deviations from design:** [none / description]"

Also update `README.md` in the project root:
- Add or update bullet points in the **Features** section to reflect user-visible changes introduced by the feature; keep the same terse, benefit-focused style as the existing bullets

Also update the living system docs at `docs/specs/`:
- **`requirements.md`** — add or extend sections to reflect new endpoints, UI behaviour, or constraints introduced by the feature; do not duplicate the feature's own `02-requirements.md`, just integrate the net-new facts into the existing document structure
- **`design.md`** — add or extend sections to reflect new files, components, data flows, or architectural decisions; keep the same level of detail as the surrounding prose

Also update `CHANGELOG.md` in the project root:
- Determine the next version number (increment minor for new features, patch for fixes)
- Prepend a new version entry in reverse-chronological order with the format `## [x.y.z] — YYYY-MM-DD`
- Under the entry, write a short bullet list of user-visible changes (not file names — what the user gains)
- Add a link to the feature's `07-changes.md` for full details
- Keep the table of contents at the top in sync — add a link to the new version entry

`CHANGELOG.md` structure:
```markdown
# Changelog

## Table of Contents

- [x.y.z — YYYY-MM-DD](#xyz--yyyy-mm-dd)

---

## [x.y.z] — YYYY-MM-DD

- [bullet list of user-visible changes]

[Full change log →](docs/specs/features/<feature-name>/07-changes.md)
```

## Phase 8 — Commit

**Model: `claude-haiku-5-5`** — Haiku runs the checks and stages the commit.

Run type-check and lint before committing. Stage only relevant files (never secrets or scratch files). Do not add any model co-authoring phrases. Show the proposed commit message and get confirmation.

Do not include a Co-Authored-By phrase.

> "Checks pass. Proposed commit:
> `[type(scope): short description]`
> Shall I commit?"

[↑ Back to top](#feature-development-workflow)

---

## Phase 9 — PR

**Model: `claude-haiku-5-5`** — Haiku drafts the PR description from the change log and commit history.

Only create a PR when the user says it's ready. Do not add any model co-authoring phrases. Draft a PR description with summary and test plan, then ask before pushing.

> "Ready to open a PR? Here's the draft:
> **Title:** [title]
> **Summary:** [bullets]
> **Test plan:** [checklist]
> Shall I push the branch and open it?"

After the PR is opened:

1. **Wait for checks to start** — pause ~15 seconds after opening, then run `gh pr checks <number>` to see if any CI workflows were triggered.
2. **Poll until complete** — if checks are running, re-run `gh pr checks <number> --watch` (or loop with a reasonable interval) until all checks reach a terminal state (`pass`, `fail`, or `skipped`).
3. **All checks pass** — show the PR URL and move to Phase 9.
4. **Any check fails** — report which check(s) failed and their log URL, then return to **Phase 5 — Implement** to fix the issue(s). After fixes are committed (Phase 8), re-open the PR phase from the push step and repeat the check-watch cycle.
5. **No checks present** — if `gh pr checks` reports no checks after the initial pause, proceed directly to Phase 9.

> "Checks passed ✓ — PR is ready: [PR URL]"
>
> or
>
> "Check `[name]` failed. Returning to Phase 5 to fix the issue before the PR can merge."

[↑ Back to top](#feature-development-workflow)

---

## Phase 10 — Close

Before doing anything, confirm the PR has been merged. Check with `gh pr view <number> --json mergedAt,state` and stop if it has not been merged yet.

Once merge is confirmed:

1. Check out the main branch: `git checkout main && git pull`
2. Confirm the local feature branch to delete, then ask the user before deleting it: `git branch -d feature/<name>`

> "PR #[number] is merged. I'll switch to `main` and pull the latest.
> Can I delete the local branch `feature/<name>`?"
